"Fine! Treat me like I'm six!" Mehak's door banged, rattling the calendar pinned to it. Gargi stood in the corridor of their Lucknow flat, the argument about the late-night concert still hanging in the air.
Two hours later the door creaked open. Mehak shuffled into the kitchen in her socks, where Gargi was packing tomorrow's lunch dabbas.
"Mumma, I'm still angry about the concert," she said. "But can I tell you something else?"
Gargi put the lid down. "Tell me."
"Shruti's parents are splitting up. She cried in the school washroom today and I didn't know what to say to her."
Gargi pulled out a stool. Mehak sat with her knees up, and the concert argument waited for another day.

qa.a: She put the lid down and said "Tell me", setting the argument aside to listen, which kept the door open.

qa.a: She may feel relieved and touched that the fight hasn't stopped her daughter from turning to her.

"I'm sixteen, Mama. I can pick my own subjects."
"And I'm allowed an opinion, Tanvir."
"Your opinion is always the same!" He grabbed his headphones and stamped upstairs.
Half an hour later he was back in the kitchen doorway. Gurpreet was rolling rotis.
"Mama... you got a minute?"
"For you, always. Even when you're shouting."
"I got nine out of forty in the physics test. Everyone thinks I'm the smart one."
Gurpreet wiped her hands. "That must have felt awful to carry all week."
"It did."
"Want to sit? You can talk while I burn these."
He almost smiled. "You never burn them."
"Tonight I might. Tell me what happened in the test."
He pulled out a chair. "And I'm still picking my own subjects."
"We'll argue about that tomorrow."

qa.a: He got nine out of forty in the physics test.

qa.q: What was Tanvir worried about when he mentioned the test?
qa.a: He was worried about letting people down, because everyone thinks he is the smart one.

qa.q: What turning point shows the bond is safe, and why?
qa.a: Tanvir walks back in to tell his mother about the test right after their fight, and she listens instead of scoring a point, so the argument doesn't shut the door.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet seem to see Tanvir's push to choose his own subjects?
qa.a: She seems to accept it calmly as something to argue about later; what matters to her is that he still comes to her when things go wrong.

"I still think you're unfair about the curfew."

"It's Leela. Her family's moving to Guwahati next month. That's why I'm at her place every evening. I just want the time with her."

passage:
Last winter I fought with Amma for a whole week about the school trek. She said it was too far; I said she treated me like a baby. I slammed my door more than once. I went anyway, with her grudging permission and about fifty rules.
Then, in January, my best friend group split up over something stupid, and I got left out of everything. I didn't post about it. I didn't sulk in my room either.
I went to the kitchen where Amma was chopping onions, sat on the counter and said, "Can I tell you something bad?"
She put the knife down. "Always, Mridul."
We talked till the dal burned. We still argue about curfews. But I know that when things go wrong, I can walk into that kitchen, fight or no fight.

qa.q: What did Mridul and Amma fight about for a week?
qa.a: The school trek.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when the friend group split up?
qa.a: Mridul felt hurt and left out, and trusted Amma enough to go to the kitchen and ask, "Can I tell you something bad?"

qa.q: What does the passage show about arguing and staying close?
qa.a: Mridul can push for independence and argue about treks and curfews, and still go home to talk when troubled, because the bond survives the fights.

qa.q: How might Amma feel when Mridul asks to tell her something bad?
qa.a: Amma likely feels glad and trusted, since she put the knife down at once and said "Always," even after their week of fighting.

grounding: Shows a teen who argues for independence with a parent yet still turns to her when troubled, trusting the bond survives disagreement.
